paragraphs: This paper changes what a feedforward network treats as adjustable during learning. Its cost function depends explicitly on the internal representation as well as the connection weights. The internal representation is the pattern of hidden activity through which the network connects its inputs to its outputs. Making that representation part of the objective exposes another part of the learning problem.

The authors reformulate training as two simple perceptron problems together with a search for suitable internal representations. This separates finding useful hidden states from adjusting the connections associated with them. Backpropagation appears as a limiting case, so the proposed method also provides a broader formulation that includes a familiar learning procedure.

The reported advantage concerns how often training finds a successful solution. Success is more frequent than with backpropagation when weights and hidden units are updated on the same timescale, once per learning step. This supports the value of jointly adjusting representations and weights under that update arrangement; it does not establish a universal improvement across all training conditions.
neurips-1989-a-cost-function-for-interna.tldr: A learning objective that explicitly includes hidden representations finds successful solutions more often than backpropagation under the reported update schedule.

paragraphs: The paper presents a neural algorithm for recognizing patterns as signals unfold over time. Training happens online in a single pass and needs only one representative template for each class. This combines rapid setup with temporal matching: the system must identify an evolving signal while data continue to arrive.

A central concern is recognition under difficult noise conditions. The algorithm continuously adapts to changes in background noise, handles brief signals with low signal-to-noise ratios, and accommodates non-Gaussian noise. It also uses contextual dependencies and produces Bayesian probability estimates. These features connect the recognition decision to both surrounding information and uncertainty, rather than reducing the output to an unexplained class label.

The authors adapt the algorithm to passive sonar detection and classification and run it on a Connection Machine. They report correct classification within 500 milliseconds of signal onset for signals embedded in noise and subject to considerable uncertainty. The result demonstrates the combination of timely decisions, limited training examples, and adaptation in the stated sonar application.
neurips-1989-a-neural-network-for-real-t.tldr: An online neural algorithm recognizes noisy temporal signals from single training templates, with reported sonar classifications within 500 milliseconds of onset.

paragraphs: This paper describes an analog neural chip whose connections can be rearranged to support different network layouts. It integrates 1,024 distributed-neuron synapses in a 6.1 by 3.3 millimeter active area. Groups of sixteen synapses form tiles, with programmable switch matrices placed between them.

The switches allow the same hardware resources to implement different layer arrangements, including 12–32–12 and 16–12–12–16 networks, or two 12–32 networks. The numbers specify units per layer, including inputs. Providing this flexibility adds a reported 15 percent area overhead. The design therefore makes network structure a programmable choice within the resources available on the chip.

Weights are stored as analog values on MOS capacitors and are usable at a resolution of one percent of their full-scale value. Charge injected by access switches and charge leakage set this limit. Gain and the shape of the nonlinearity are also programmable. Together, these features show how reconfiguration can extend beyond wiring to the numerical behavior of an analog network, while remaining constrained by physical storage effects.
neurips-1989-a-reconfigurable-analog-vls.tldr: A tiled analog neural chip supports multiple network configurations through programmable switches, with additional control over weights, gain, and nonlinear response.

paragraphs: The paper addresses an associative memory used within a learning control system called LERNAS. The software memory is based on the CHAC storage scheme. Its relevant property is local generalization: information associated with one input can also influence nearby inputs through an area of interpolation.

The authors identify a restriction in this arrangement. The extent of local generalization is fixed, so the memory uses a predetermined interpolation area. That extent matters because it governs how broadly stored information applies beyond the particular inputs already represented. A fixed setting makes the reach of generalization part of the original design rather than something the memory can organize for itself.

The proposed contribution is an algorithm for self-organizing, variable generalization, drawing on ideas from Kohonen. It targets the associative memory component of the control loop by making its generalization behavior adjustable. The significance is the shift from a fixed interpolation area toward an organized, variable one. The supplied description presents this algorithmic direction without claiming a particular improvement in control accuracy or learning speed.
neurips-1989-a-self-organizing-associati.tldr: A Kohonen-inspired algorithm gives an associative memory for learning control a self-organizing, variable range of local generalization.

paragraphs: The paper explores recognizing three-dimensional objects by storing several two-dimensional views of each object. Its network has two layers of units that sum their inputs and apply a threshold. This gives the system a way to represent an object through distinct appearances associated with different viewpoints.

Using unsupervised Hebbian relaxation, the network learns to recognize ten objects across viewpoints. Training produces compact representations of the particular views it encounters. The important connection is between organizing individual views and recognizing the objects they depict: the learned representation must accommodate changes in appearance while supporting object recognition.

When shown previously unseen views of the same objects, the network exhibits substantial generalization. Its recognition ability therefore extends beyond the specific views presented during training. In simulated psychophysical experiments, its behavior also resembles human behavior qualitatively. That resemblance concerns the pattern of behavior rather than a stated numerical match. Together, the findings support multiple stored views as a useful basis for recognition across changes in viewpoint.
neurips-1989-a-self-organizing-multiple-.tldr: A two-layer network learns compact representations of object views and generalizes to unseen viewpoints of the same objects.

paragraphs: This paper targets the computational work required to train nonlinear neural networks whose responses evolve dynamically. Supervised learning needs information about how parameter changes affect the network response and its objective. Computing that information can be expensive when many parameters influence the same evolving system.

The proposed method uses adjoint operators to organize the sensitivity calculation. By solving one appropriately constructed set of linear equations, it obtains information about response changes caused by perturbations in all system parameters. The practical idea is to share the mathematical work across parameters, so that a single coordinated calculation supplies the information needed for learning.

The abstract states a lower bound of O(N²) on the speedup per learning iteration over conventional methods for calculating the energy gradient, where N is the neuron count. This is a claim about the cost of a learning iteration, rather than the number of iterations needed to finish training. The contribution is an efficient route to gradient information for dynamical networks.
neurips-1989-adjoint-operator-algorithms.tldr: An adjoint-based method computes parameter sensitivities through one linear system, with a stated O(N²) lower bound on per-iteration speedup.

paragraphs: The vestibulo-ocular reflex stabilizes images on the retina by producing compensatory eye movements during rapid head motion. Its main pathways carry signals from the semicircular canals to the eye movement system. The paper focuses on how this largely feedforward mechanism can adapt so that its movements remain appropriately matched to head motion.

Visual feedback does not directly enter the reflex computation described here. Instead, motor learning must keep the response calibrated. The model the authors build on uses retinal image slip to adjust reflex gain, meaning the strength of the eye movement response. This separates the immediate generation of movement from the information used to adapt that response.

The authors design and test analog VLSI circuitry implementing a simplified version of Lisberger's adaptive model. The contribution is a physical circuit realization of the proposed adaptation mechanism. It links a biological control problem to an analog hardware implementation, showing how a simplified model of visually guided calibration can be embodied in circuitry.
neurips-1989-an-analog-vlsi-model-of-ada.tldr: Analog circuitry implements a simplified model that uses retinal image slip to adapt the strength of compensatory eye movements.

paragraphs: The paper studies how feature-sensitive receptive fields form in a three-layer feedforward network for visual processing. A receptive field describes the pattern of input to which a cell responds. The authors derive analytic solutions to an information-theoretic equation governing how connection strengths evolve, making the resulting receptive-field structure mathematically explicit.

Their first result connects receptive fields to the eigenvector associated with the largest eigenvalue of a derived Fredholm integral equation. In plain language, the equation identifies a dominant mathematical pattern, and that pattern determines the feature-analyzing cell's receptive field. This links the structure that emerges in the network to the governing learning equation.

The analysis also identifies symmetry breaking, described as parity violation, as the mechanism behind changes in receptive-field shape. The authors explicitly specify conditions under which different shapes form. These results move from describing possible receptive fields to explaining their formation: both the dominant pattern and the changes between forms are tied to properties of the mathematical model.
neurips-1989-analytic-solutions-to-the-f.tldr: Analytic solutions connect visual receptive-field formation to a dominant eigenvector and identify symmetry breaking as a cause of changes in shape.

paragraphs: This paper shows how an oscillating cortical model can function as an associative memory. Its architecture contains excitatory neurons with local inhibitory feedback, creating nonlinear oscillators. Long-range connections between these oscillators are exclusively excitatory. The authors motivate this minimal coupling arrangement using known anatomy.

A local Hebb-like rule adjusts primary and higher-order synapses at the ends of the long-range connections. Through this learning rule, the network stores patterns of oscillation amplitudes of the kinds observed in olfactory and visual cortex. Memory is therefore expressed through structured rhythmic activity, rather than requiring every stored pattern to be a fixed, unchanging state.

The rule comes from a more general projection algorithm for recurrent analog networks. That algorithm analytically guarantees content-addressable storage of continuous periodic sequences without spurious attractors. The stated capacity is N/2 Fourier components for N nodes, counting components of periodic signals rather than simply counting memories. The result connects an anatomically motivated oscillator network with a mathematical account of reliable storage.
neurips-1989-associative-memory-in-a-sim.tldr: An anatomically motivated oscillator network stores rhythmic activity patterns using a local learning rule derived from a guaranteed periodic-memory construction.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes a perceptron's classification ability when inputs have finite precision. Its positive result rests on a specific probabilistic setting: there are n uniformly distributed pattern vectors, each represented by cn bits, with c greater than one. Under those conditions, the perceptron can realize every possible binary labeling of the patterns with high probability.

The storage result compares the resulting network with keeping the full input patterns. The network needs a proportion O(log n/n) of that storage, which shrinks as n increases. Thus, in the stated setting, representing a classification through the network can require a progressively smaller fraction of the memory needed to retain all patterns explicitly.

The authors also report O(n²) arithmetic operations for the perceptron algorithm with high probability, alongside an O(n^3.5) worst-case bound for methods such as linear programming. Those bounds use different probability qualifications, which matters when interpreting the comparison. The paper further identifies mathematical connections to VLSI circuit testing and random matrix theory.
neurips-1989-complexity-of-finite-precis.tldr: Under a uniform random finite-precision input model, a perceptron can realize all binary labelings with high probability while using compact storage.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether computational efficiency can help explain the spatial organization of neural responses. Particular brain regions contain organized maps, but the motivating problem is how to relate a map's structure to the computation performed there. Observing spatial order alone does not supply that relationship.

The authors approach the question through parallel computers. When a computation is distributed among multiple processors, arrangements resembling brain maps can emerge. This provides a setting in which to examine maps together with the computations assigned to them. The analogy directs attention to how the organization of processing relates to the work being carried out.

The paper discusses this relationship in parallel computing and suggests that similar considerations may apply to the brain. Its contribution is a proposed organizing perspective: brain maps might be understood partly through the computational demands they serve. The abstract presents that connection as a suggestion, so the significance lies in framing a possible explanation for spatial organization rather than establishing a general law of brain mapping.
neurips-1989-computational-efficiency-a-.tldr: The paper proposes using the relationship between processor maps and computation to investigate why brain responses are spatially organized.

paragraphs: The paper investigates rhythmic, correlated neural activity in the cerebral cortex. Such oscillations have been observed in both olfactory and primary visual regions. The authors develop models of these two systems that reproduce their observed oscillatory properties, giving them a computational setting for examining how the rhythms arise.

They use the models to study how oscillations depend on individual cell properties and network architecture. These are related but distinct sources of behavior: a cell's response characteristics affect its own activity, while the arrangement of connections affects how activity is coordinated across the network. Studying both helps connect local mechanisms with collective rhythms.

The authors discuss the possibility that oscillatory events reflect architectural properties shared across the cortex. They also suggest that these rhythms may help coordinate neural activity during sensory processing. Reproducing oscillatory properties in the models supports investigation of these ideas, while the broader role of rhythms is presented as a proposed interpretation. The work connects simulated network dynamics to questions about sensory coordination.
neurips-1989-computer-simulation-of-osci.tldr: Models of olfactory and visual cortex reproduce oscillatory behavior and explore how cellular properties and network architecture shape those rhythms.

paragraphs: This paper connects probabilistic models used in computer vision with neural network computation. The starting point is the Markov random field, which represents interacting quantities whose values must be inferred together. The abstract highlights reconstructing surfaces from sparse, noisy depth measurements and combining early vision processes to identify physical discontinuities.

The authors apply mean field theory to these models and obtain a class of neural networks. The significance is the translation between a model of the inference problem and a network that can help solve it. The network arises from applying the mathematical method to the random field, linking its computation to the original formulation.

The resulting networks can speed up solving the Markov random field models. This makes the approach relevant to vision problems where incomplete or noisy observations must be reconciled across a structured representation. The authors also state that the method extends beyond computer vision. Its broader contribution is therefore a route from interacting probabilistic models to neural computational procedures.
neurips-1989-coupled-markov-random-field.tldr: Applying mean field theory to Markov random fields produces neural networks that can accelerate their solution in vision and other domains.

paragraphs: The paper considers a robot learning an unfamiliar environment by acting and observing what happens. Its internal model should predict the consequences of actions and support choosing action sequences that reach a goal. The central task is therefore to discover how the environment responds, rather than simply record individual observations.

Earlier symbolic work represented finite-state environments using an update graph and paired that representation with strategic exploration. The authors implement the update graph in a highly specialized neural architecture. They train it with backpropagation while using random actions for exploration, combining a structured model representation with a simple way of collecting experience.

On simple problems, the neural implementation can outperform the symbolic algorithm despite its random exploration strategy. It can also accommodate stochastic environments, where an action's consequences need not be completely predictable. The authors emphasize another benefit: expressing update graphs as networks suggests generalizations that are less apparent from a symbolic perspective. The approach thus offers both an implementation and a direction for extending the representation.
neurips-1989-discovering-the-structure-o.tldr: A specialized neural update graph learns environmental structure through random exploration and can outperform a symbolic approach on simple problems.

paragraphs: This paper empirically examines how the number of adjustable weights in a feedforward network relates to generalization. The concern is whether a network's learned classification behavior carries over beyond its training examples. Parameter count is the design variable under study, connecting network size to the reliability of learned decisions.

The authors use two experimental settings. One consists of simulated continuous-valued data with controlled properties, including signal-to-noise ratio. The other uses real speech represented by vector-quantized mel cepstra. In both settings, backpropagation trains the network to distinguish among multiple classes. The combination places the parameter question in both a controlled data setting and a speech application.

The paper reports the studies and demonstrates cross-validation techniques for preventing overfitting. Cross-validation makes performance on held-out data part of the assessment, rather than relying solely on how well training examples are fitted. The stated contribution is an empirical investigation of network size together with a practical method for controlling overfitting; the abstract does not assert a single optimal parameter count.
neurips-1989-generalization-and-paramete.tldr: Experiments on simulated data and real speech examine network size and demonstrate cross-validation as a way to prevent overfitting.

paragraphs: The paper applies a network trained by backpropagation to recognizing handwritten digits. Its inputs are normalized images containing individual digits. This defines the recognition problem clearly: the network receives an already isolated digit image and must determine which digit it represents.

The system requires little preprocessing, but its network architecture is strongly constrained and designed specifically for the task. That pairing is the central design choice. Task knowledge enters through the organization of the network, while learning adjusts its parameters from examples. The result illustrates how a carefully chosen architecture can accompany relatively modest preparation of the image data.

On ZIP code digits supplied by the U.S. Postal Service, the method reports a one percent error rate and approximately a nine percent rejection rate. Rejection means some inputs are left without an accepted classification, so both figures matter when judging the result. The reported performance combines successful digit recognition with the option to decline a decision on part of the input set.
neurips-1989-handwritten-digit-recogniti.tldr: A task-specific backpropagation network recognizes isolated postal digits with a reported one percent error rate and roughly nine percent rejection rate.

paragraphs: The paper explores two ways to combine neural classifiers with Hidden Markov Model speech recognizers. The shared aim is to improve discrimination between speech patterns while preserving the HMM's handling of temporal structure. The two approaches place the neural network at different stages of recognition.

In the first, a neural classifier performs additional discrimination after the HMM recognizer. On a small-vocabulary task, both radial basis function and backpropagation networks substantially reduce errors; the radial basis function system lowers the rate from 7.9 percent to 4.2 percent. On a larger-vocabulary task, neural classifiers do not reduce recognition error, although they outperform Gaussian, Gaussian mixture, and nearest-neighbor classifiers.

In the second approach, networks extract low-level acoustic-phonetic features. Radial basis function classifiers outperform Gaussian mixtures when classifying phonemes from individual ten-millisecond frames. However, the difference becomes small when scores are accumulated across complete phonetic segments with a single-node HMM. The findings show that gains in local discrimination depend on how those decisions are integrated over time.
neurips-1989-hmm-speech-recognition-with.tldr: Neural classifiers improve some HMM speech-recognition decisions, but the gains vary with vocabulary size and temporal aggregation.

paragraphs: This paper develops graphical tools for examining layered neural networks as they learn. The tools cover both static information and dynamic behavior. A static view shows the system at a particular point, while a dynamic view makes change during learning part of what the researcher can inspect.

The visual designs use spatial arrangement, size, color, and animation. These provide several ways to present information that would otherwise need to be interpreted through numerical descriptions. Animation is especially relevant to the stated goal of understanding learning dynamics, because it lets a display communicate a process unfolding rather than only its final state.

The authors apply the tools to backpropagation networks learning simple Boolean predicates, which are rules producing true-or-false answers. They report gaining new insights into the learning process from these visualizations. The contribution is therefore an investigative method: graphical representations help researchers study how training proceeds. The reported outcome concerns understanding network behavior, rather than a change to the learning algorithm or a claim of improved prediction accuracy.
neurips-1989-neural-network-visualizatio.tldr: Graphics using space, size, color, and animation reveal aspects of backpropagation learning dynamics on simple Boolean tasks.

paragraphs: The paper describes an attempt to apply Edelman's Neuronal Group Selection principle to a real robotic manipulator with two links. The target is a simple perception-action task, bringing a proposed principle of neural organization into contact with the demands of controlling a physical mechanism.

The authors begin by motivating an alternative to the position-control approach of classical robotics. They look toward a primitive animal limb control mode described as neurologically ballistic. This provides the biological direction for their investigation: the question is how an alternative organization of control might coordinate what the system perceives with how it acts.

Their proposed route is selectionist, using Neuronal Group Selection as the organizing idea for that coordination. The abstract presents the work as an ongoing attempt rather than a completed demonstration of superior control. Its contribution is the grounding of a neural theory in a concrete robotics problem, where the theory must support a relationship between perception and movement in an actual two-link arm.
neurips-1989-neuronal-group-selection-th.tldr: The paper investigates Neuronal Group Selection as an organizing principle for perception and action in a real two-link robot arm.

paragraphs: This paper presents compact CMOS synapse circuits that operate directly on asynchronous pulse streams. The proposed circuits use only three or four MOS transistors per synapse. Neural activity is represented by how frequently pulses occur, while pulse magnitude remains constant. This takes inspiration from the pulse-based signaling of biological neurons.

Each synapse uses incoming pulses to increase or decrease the receiving neuron's activity. The sender's activity determines how often the changes occur, and the synaptic weight determines their size. The representation and arithmetic therefore work together: the timing of events carries the sender's state, while the connection controls their effect on the receiver.

The authors describe chips containing more than one hundred fully programmable synapses and project designs toward networks with hundreds of neurons. These are different scales of claim: the synapse chips are described implementations, while the larger neuron networks are projections. The significance lies in the compact synapse circuit and its direct processing of pulses, providing a hardware basis for the proposed expansion.
neurips-1989-pulse-firing-neural-chips-f.tldr: Compact programmable synapse circuits compute directly on asynchronous pulses, with implemented chips supporting projections toward networks of hundreds of neurons.

paragraphs: This paper presents two neural architectures for chunking symbolic rewrite rules. Rewrite rules describe transformations between symbolic expressions, and chunking concerns how such rule-based material is organized into learned units. The task connects an explicitly symbolic form of knowledge with representations learned by a neural system.

One architecture uses backpropagation, while the other uses competitive learning. Both are developed for the same kinds of rules, which gives the comparison a common target. The distinction is therefore not simply that the systems address different symbolic tasks; they bring different learning approaches and representations to a shared category of task.

The authors report differences in both representational ability and learning behavior. Those are separate considerations: what a system can represent need not be the same question as how it acquires that representation. The paper's stated contribution is this comparison between two connectionist approaches to rule chunking. It highlights that choosing a neural architecture for symbolic material involves considering the representation it supports as well as its learning procedure.
neurips-1989-rule-representations-in-a-c.tldr: Two neural approaches to chunking symbolic rewrite rules differ in both what they can represent and how they learn.

paragraphs: The paper investigates combining neural learning with speech-science knowledge to recognize speech across speakers. That knowledge informs several parts of the system: preprocessing, input and output coding, supervision, and architectural constraints. The approach makes domain knowledge part of the design through which the network learns.

To handle speech over time, the authors combine delays with copies of hidden and output activations supplied at the input. They also use Back-Propagation for Sequences, a learning algorithm for networks with local self-loops. These mechanisms let the system incorporate temporal information, which matters because speech recognition depends on how acoustic evidence develops across a sequence.

The strategy is demonstrated in several experiments. The highlighted result concerns distinguishing nasal speech sounds, where applying a hypothesis from speech theory dramatically improves generalization. This finding supports the value of combining learned processing with task-specific knowledge in the reported setting. The evidence links the improvement to a particular speech-theory intervention, rather than claiming that every use of domain knowledge necessarily helps.
neurips-1989-speaker-independent-speech-.tldr: Speech-science knowledge and temporal neural processing are combined, with a reported large generalization improvement on nasal-sound discrimination.

paragraphs: Cascade-Correlation learns both a network's parameters and its structure. It starts with a minimal network, then trains and adds hidden units one at a time. Adding these units gradually creates a multilayer network, allowing its size and topology to emerge during supervised learning.

Once a hidden unit is installed, its incoming weights are frozen. It becomes a permanent feature detector that can help produce outputs or serve as input to more complex detectors. This addresses what the authors call the moving target problem: when many weights change simultaneously, hidden units must learn useful roles in a continually changing internal environment.

The authors report much faster learning than backpropagation on the problems they examined. They also emphasize that learned structures remain available when the training set changes and that training does not require propagating error signals backward through the network's connections. The central idea is cumulative construction: preserve an acquired feature, then build additional features around it as learning continues.
neurips-1989-the-cascade-correlation-lea.tldr: Cascade-Correlation grows a network by adding and preserving learned feature detectors, reporting faster learning than backpropagation on the examined problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies how hardware constraints affect a self-organizing feature map used in speech preprocessing. The authors assess the consequences through the error rate of the complete speech recognition system. This connects circuit design choices to the performance of the application that depends on them.

The study varies weight precision, adaptation precision, distance measures, and approximations reflecting device characteristics and manufacturing variability. Experiments use the TI isolated-word database with sixteen speakers. Recognition performance degrades when weight precision falls below eight bits, identifying a concrete precision constraint in the tested system.

The authors also find that the algorithm's competitive operation relaxes requirements for uniformity and linearity. That tolerance supports their assessment that the method is well suited to fully analog implementation. Prototype circuits are fabricated and characterized using constraints established in simulation. The work therefore connects algorithm-level experiments with circuit development: it identifies a sensitivity to weight precision while showing room for flexibility in other physical characteristics.
neurips-1989-the-effects-of-circuit-inte.tldr: Hardware-oriented speech experiments reveal degradation below eight-bit weight precision while supporting analog implementation through tolerance of circuit nonuniformity and nonlinearity.

paragraphs: The paper describes the design and testing of a neural associative memory implemented as a programmable chip. The system is called exponential correlation associative memory, or ECAM. Associative recall retrieves a stored pattern through its relationship to a presented pattern, making the recall computation central to the memory's design.

The prototype uses a three-micrometer CMOS process and can store thirty-two patterns, each containing twenty-four bits. Its capacity is attributed partly to special neurons that perform exponentiation. The circuit implements those neurons using MOS transistors operating below threshold. This connects a particular mathematical operation in the memory model to a physical transistor implementation.

The tested chip performs one associative recall in three microseconds. Together with the stated storage capacity, this provides a concrete account of what the prototype can do. The contribution brings the ECAM design into hardware and demonstrates its recall operation. It also shows how the implementation of the exponentiation neurons contributes to the memory architecture's stated capacity.
neurips-1989-vlsi-implementation-of-a-hi.tldr: A programmable ECAM chip stores thirty-two 24-bit patterns and performs associative recall in three microseconds using specialized exponentiation neurons.
